front: [Chain: EURFUT 1/3] Context: Euro-Bund future, notional €100,000, notional coupon 6%, deliverable bonds with 8.5 to 10.5 years remaining, minimum price change 0.01 (€10). Approximate the CTD by a 6% annual-coupon 9-year bond at a 2.50% yield. What is the EUR DV01 per contract and what yield move does one tick correspond to?
back:
Headline: about €93 per bp per contract; one tick (€10) is about 0.11 bp of CTD yield.
Working: price of the approximating bond \(P=127.90\) per 100. Its price sensitivity is \(\partial P/\partial y \approx -0.0928\) per 100 per bp, i.e. modified duration \(\approx 7.3\) (\(0.0928/127.9\cdot 10^4\)). Contract value is \(P/100\times€100{,}000\), so DV01 \(\approx 0.000928\times€100{,}000 = €92.8\) per bp.
Tick: \(€10/€92.8 \approx 0.108\) bp.
Why it matters: the futures DV01 is a CTD DV01 divided by the CTD conversion factor, so the desk's hedge is sensitive to which bond is cheapest to deliver, not to the index.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the one-tick yield equivalent a function of the CTD's duration rather than of the coupon? Answer: the tick is a fixed price amount, so the yield equivalent is tick divided by DV01, and DV01 scales with price times modified duration.

front: [Chain: EURFUT 2/3] Context: Euro-Buxl future, notional €100,000, 4% notional coupon, deliverable bonds with 24.0 to 35.0 years remaining, minimum price change 0.02 (€20). Approximate the CTD by a 4% annual-coupon 30-year bond at a 3.00% yield. What is the EUR DV01 per contract, and what is the yield-equivalent of one tick? Compare with the Bund.
back:
Headline: about €221 per bp per contract, roughly 2.4 times the Bund; one tick (€20) is about 0.09 bp.
Working: price \(P=119.60\). Price sensitivity per bp \(\approx 0.0221\) per 100, so DV01 \(\approx 0.00221\times€100{,}000 = €221\). Tick yield-equivalent \(=€20/€221 \approx 0.090\) bp.
Ratio to the Bund: \(221/92.8 \approx 2.38\), the duration ratio of a 30-year against a 9-year approximating bond in the same yield regime.
Trade-off: the Buxl gives a lot more DV01 per contract, so a DV01-matched hedge needs fewer contracts, but its CTD set is small (few deliverable bonds at 24 to 35 years), so basis and squeeze risk concentrate in one or two bonds.
Interviewer follow-up: The Buxl tick is about 0.09 bp against about 0.11 bp for the Bund, so the price tick is finer in yield terms on the Buxl even though its DV01 is 2.4 times larger. Why? Answer: the tick is a fixed price amount, and a long-dated contract has so much more price sensitivity per bp that each unit of price stands for less yield.

front: [Chain: EURFUT 3/3] Context: Schatz, Bobl and Bund futures approximated by 6% annual-coupon bonds of 2, 5 and 9 years at yields 2.00%, 2.30% and 2.50%. Per contract DV01s are about €20.6, €51.7 and €92.8. You trade a DV01-neutral 2s5s9s butterfly: short one Bobl (belly), long Schatz and Bund wings with equal DV01 in each wing. How many Schatz and Bund contracts per Bobl, and what is the P&L if the 5-year yield alone rises 5 bp?
back:
Headline: about 1.26 Schatz and 0.28 Bund per Bobl; a 5 bp belly-only rise makes the fly gain about €258.5.
Working: belly DV01 = €51.7. Each wing carries half: €25.9. Schatz contracts \(=25.9/20.6 \approx 1.26\). Bund contracts \(=25.9/92.8 \approx 0.28\). Check: \(1.26\times20.6+0.28\times92.8 \approx 51.7\).
P&L: the short Bobl gains when its yield rises and its price falls. \(5\times€51.7 = +€258.5\). Wings unchanged.
Where it breaks: equal-DV01 wings are level-neutral, not curve-neutral. A parallel shift gives zero, but a 2s-versus-9s slope move with the belly fixed has no offset. The yield betas across the three tenors are not one, so a hedge that uses the CTD-based DV01 is only approximate.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the desk prefer a 1:1 Schatz-to-Bobl ratio in some curve trades? Answer: it is a notional-based convention. The DV01-based ratio is what keeps the level exposure flat.
Position DV01 by leg of the 2s5s9s fly: 1.26 Schatz and 0.28 Bund per Bobl

front: Cloze: the Euro-Bund future has notional {{c1::€100,000}}, a notional coupon of {{c2::6%}}, deliverable bonds with {{c3::8.5 to 10.5}} years remaining, and a minimum price change of 0.01 worth {{c4::€10}}.
back: Source: Eurex futures and option contract pages list the Bund underlying terms (remaining term 8.5 to 10.5 years, 6% notional coupon). The €100,000 contract size and the March/June/September/December cycle are in the Eurex specification as listed by Barchart. The 0.01 minimum price change (€10) is in the Eurex contract-specification history. Check the current Eurex specification before quoting.

front: Cloze: the Euro-Buxl future has a notional coupon of {{c1::4%}}, deliverable bonds with {{c2::24.0 to 35.0}} years remaining, and a minimum price change of 0.02 worth {{c3::€20}}, so one tick is about {{c4::0.09 bp}} of yield at a 30-year DV01 of about €221 per bp.
back: Current Eurex Euro-Buxl terms: 4% notional coupon, 24.0 to 35.0 years remaining, minimum price change 0.02 worth €20. Yield-equivalent is \(20/221\approx 0.09\) bp. Some older Eurex documents quote a €10 unit; use the current contract page.

front: Cloze: the Euro-Bund futures last trading day is {{c1::two exchange days}} before the delivery day, which is the {{c2::10th calendar day}} of the delivery month (or the next exchange day if that is not an exchange day), and trading in the maturing contract ends on that last trading day.
back: Delivery day: the 10th calendar day of the quarter-end delivery month, or the next exchange day if that is not one. Last trading day: two exchange days before the delivery day. Source: Eurex fixed-income rulebook history (2013 version, as cited by Barchart and MarketsWiki); no current Eurex page was retrieved. The closing time on the last trading day could not be confirmed in a current Eurex source, so it is not on this card.

front: [Chain: BTP_BUND 1/3] Context: illustrative 10-year yields, BTP at 3.70% and Bund at 2.60%, so the outright spread is 110 bp. Decompose this spread into the components a rates-credit desk would separate. Why do you compare asset-swap spreads rather than yields, and what does the comparison still leave in the number?
back:
Headline: the 110 bp is not a single credit premium. Separate (i) sovereign credit and fiscal-risk premium, (ii) liquidity and market-depth premium, (iii) supply and index/ownership effects (bank and insurance holdings, index weights), (iv) ECB-related effects (asset purchases, the TPI as a conditional backstop).
Why ASW: yields differ by coupon, maturity, repo-specialness and convexity. Asset-swap spreads (BTP and Bund both against the same EUR swap curve) remove the coupon and tenor mismatch and most of the common curve. The residual swap-basis difference between Italian and German swap spreads is small but not zero.
What is left: the ASW difference still carries the country-specific risk premium plus any liquidity and supply effects. It does not isolate default risk, since no market-implied default probability is taken out.
Interviewer follow-up: How would you test whether a widening is fiscal or liquidity? Compare the BTP-Bund ASW move with the move in the BTP bid-ask and the ASW move of other high-beta sovereigns (for example France or Spain), since a common-factor move points to contagion rather than Italy-specific news.
Decomposition of the 110 bp BTP-Bund outright into asset-swap and residual components

front: [Chain: BTP_BUND 2/3] Context: long €100 million BTP 10-year at 3.70% (DV01 about €82,300 per bp). You hedge with Bund 10-year at 2.60% (DV01 about €87,070 per bp on €100 million), so the DV01-neutral Bund notional is €94.6 million. The BTP-Bund spread widens 25 bp while the Bund yield is unchanged. What is the P&L of the spread trade and what is the sign of its exposure?
back:
Headline: loss of about €2.06 million; the trade is long the BTP-Bund spread.
Working: with the Bund leg unchanged, the BTP yield moves by 25 bp. P&L on the BTP leg \(= -25\times€82{,}300 \approx -€2.06\text{m}\). The Bund leg is flat, so the net is the same figure.
Check the hedge: \(94.56\text{m}\times€87{,}070/€100\text{m} \approx €82{,}300\) per bp, matching the BTP DV01. So a parallel move is hedged, and only the spread remains.
Interviewer follow-up: The DV01 match is on the 10-year point. How much of the residual is curve risk? Answer: the BTP and Bund curves have different slopes at 9 to 11 years, so a 2-year-spread move can leave a residual. Use key-rate DV01 on each leg to quantify it.

front: [Chain: BTP_BUND 3/3] Context: the DV01-neutral long BTP / short Bund package from card 2 (€100 million BTP, €94.6 million Bund, both 10-year). Ignoring funding and repo, the annual carry is 3.70% on the BTP less 2.60% on the Bund notional. What is the one-year breakeven widening, in bp, and what changes the breakeven once you add repo?
back:
Headline: breakeven widening of about 15 bp over one year, before funding.
Working: carry \(= €100\text{m}\times3.70\% - €94.56\text{m}\times2.60\% = €3.70\text{m} - €2.46\text{m} = €1.24\)m. Breakeven widening \(= \text{carry}/\text{DV01}_{BTP} = €1.24\text{m}/€82{,}300 \approx 15\) bp.
Repo: the BTP is funded in repo at its own repo rate and the Bund leg earns or pays its own repo rate. If Bund repo is special, the Bund short's cost rises and the breakeven falls; a BTP special raises the long's carry. Use the repo difference (not general collateral) in the calculation.
Where it breaks: the breakeven is a yield-based measure. A non-parallel widening (BTP 10-year moves more than the 9-year Bund CTD) changes the realised number, and an ECB-driven or fiscal jump can move the spread by many multiples of the breakeven in a few sessions.

front: Scenario: the ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) is in place as a conditional backstop for euro-area sovereign spreads that move against fundamentals. A dealer argues that this caps BTP-Bund widening, so the trade is 'long BTP-Bund with the TPI as a floor on losses'. Give the strongest objection, and state what would make the position a short option instead.
back:
Strongest objection: the TPI is a conditional, discretionary tool, not a cap or a floor. Activation needs a Governing Council judgement that market dynamics are unwarranted and disorderly, and the country must meet the criteria: compliance with the EU fiscal framework (no excessive deficit procedure), no severe macroeconomic imbalances, sustainable public debt, and sound macroeconomic policy. A widening that is judged to reflect fundamentals is not covered, which is exactly when a long spread position would lose most.
Option view: for the long BTP-Bund holder, with no support the P&L for a widening \(\Delta s\) is \(-\Delta s\). If the ECB acts above a trigger \(K\), the loss is capped at about \(K\): \(-\min(\Delta s,K)=\max(-\Delta s,-K)\), which is convex in \(\Delta s\). So the holder is long a loss cap, but only if the Council activates, and the cap is neither owned nor guaranteed.
What would make it a short option: a desk that sells widening protection to a client (a call on the spread, paying \(\max(\Delta s-K,0)\)) and counts the TPI as its hedge is short convexity, and the hedge fails in the non-activation state. Measure it with a stress on the spread at the 90th-percentile daily move, not the average.
Interviewer follow-up: What else does the TPI change? Answer: it may compress the widening tail the market prices, so market-implied spread vol should be checked against the historical distribution rather than assumed to reflect the cap.
Long BTP-Bund P&L with a TPI-style cap at a trigger K (illustrative) if activated

front: Supranational and agency (SSA) bonds: a 7-year EU-issued bond trades at a positive spread to the Bund (both on a mid-swap or ASW basis). Explain what drives the spread, why EU paper trades wide of a AAA national curve despite very strong credit, and why the spread is not a pure credit measure.
back:
Headline: the spread is mostly a liquidity and supply premium plus a funding-structure effect, not a credit premium over Germany.
Drivers: (i) issue size and index eligibility: EU bonds are large but come in many lines, so the outstanding per line can be smaller than a Bund; (ii) index-driven demand and ECB eligibility: eligibility under asset-purchase programmes affects the richness of the paper; (iii) the funding structure: EU bonds are backed by EU budget headroom rather than a single state's taxing power, which is a different legal and credit profile from a Bund; (iv) supply of new issuance in the curve, which concentrates in certain tenors.
Why not pure credit: the sovereign-to-SSA spread also embeds a coupon, liquidity and repo component. A pure credit comparison would need a CDS or an equivalent-risk basis.
Interviewer follow-up: When is an SSA cheap to the Bund? Answer: when its spread widens relative to its own history or to comparable covered paper without a corresponding change in the funding structure, so check the peer set, not just the Bund.

front: Case study: a covered bond programme with a cover pool of €120 million of mortgage loans backing €100 million of covered bonds. Overcollateralisation (OC) is pool over bonds minus 1, so OC is 20%. At origination the average LTV is 60%, so the property values are €200 million. Property prices then fall by a uniform 35% and the loans default in full in a stress. The recovery is the post-fall property value times (1 minus a 10% enforcement cost). Does the cover pool still cover the bonds? What fall in prices would exhaust the cover?
back:
Headline: yes, covered, with about a 44% fall needed to exhaust the cover in this stress.
Working: property value after a 35% fall \(=200\times0.65=130\). Average LTV is now \(120/130\approx92.3\%\), which is high but not the test. Recovery on full default \(=130\times0.90=117 \ge 100\). Covered.
Break point: set \(200(1-f)\times0.90=100\), so \(1-f=100/180\) and \(f\approx44.4\%\). Below that fall the pool shortfall starts to hit the bonds.
Where it breaks: this is a full-pool-default stress and ignores (i) time to recovery and extension risk, (ii) interest-rate mismatch in the pool, (iii) the fact that programmes usually hold OC above the statutory minimum for ratings headroom, not as the legal minimum.
Interviewer follow-up: A rating agency cuts the cover-pool credit by lifting the assumed foreclosure cost to 25%. What fall now exhausts the cover? Answer: \(200(1-f)\times0.75=100\) gives \(f=1-100/150\approx33.3\%\).
Cover pool recovery vs uniform property price fall; break-even fall about 44% (10% cost)

front: Covered bonds: explain the difference between a hard-bullet and a soft-bullet structure, and why the soft-bullet extension option is an interest-rate and liquidity risk for the bondholder rather than a credit risk. What does the investor demand for holding it?
back:
Hard bullet: principal is repaid on the scheduled maturity date. A failure to pay on that date is an event of default for the bond.
Soft bullet: if the issuer cannot repay on the maturity date from the cover pool and other resources, the maturity is extended by a defined extension period set by the programme documentation, with a new payment date. The bondholder is then exposed to a later principal date and to its reinvestment and duration profile.
Why it is not credit: the cover pool is still the source of repayment; the risk is the timing of the cash flow, which affects duration and reinvestment. An investor holding a hard bullet bears the default risk of a missed payment; the soft bullet converts that into a timing risk, and in a stressed market the extension can lengthen the bond's duration exactly when rates move.
Pricing: the soft-bullet extension is a short option for the investor. Its value rises with rate volatility and with the probability of a stressed pool, so a soft-bullet covered bond should trade wide to an otherwise identical hard-bullet bond. The difference is the compensation for that option.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a pure soft-bullet pricing approach fail in a stress? Answer: the extension is triggered by a cash-flow event, not by a price, so a model using a market-implied default probability alone misses the timing component.
Hard bullet pays on the scheduled date; soft bullet adds an extension period

front: Relative value: a 7-year covered bond on a 25 bp mid-swap spread and a 7-year SSA on a 20 bp mid-swap spread, both same currency and rating class. Under what conditions is the covered bond the cheaper asset, and what liquidity and structure adjustments would you make before comparing them?
back:
Headline: the covered bond is cheaper on paper, but the 5 bp gap is not a free pickup until adjusted for structure and liquidity.
Adjust for: (i) bullet structure (soft-bullet extension, if present) which the spread should compensate for; (ii) call and extension features; (iii) index weights and the investor base (bank-only buying vs broad index); (iv) size per line and the ability to trade in and out; (v) ECB eligibility differences; (vi) the funding and repo cost, since covered bonds can be less repo-able.
Decision rule: compare on a like-for-like duration and convexity basis, and only then judge the spread. A covered bond with a soft bullet and a thin line is cheap for a reason; a hard bullet with a broad index bid is not.
Interviewer follow-up: What single number would you put in front of a PM? Answer: the spread per year of duration (spread over duration-matched swap, with the extension option valued separately), not the raw mid-swap spread.

front: [Chain: SWAP_SPREAD 1/3] Context: 10-year SOFR par swap rate at 3.90% and 10-year Treasury yield at 4.05%, so the 10-year swap spread is minus 15 bp. Define the swap spread precisely, state which way the spread moves when the swap curve richens relative to Treasuries, and say what position is long the swap spread.
back:
Definition: swap spread \(s = S - y\), where \(S\) is the par swap rate and \(y\) the Treasury yield at the same tenor. Here \(s=3.90-4.05=-15\) bp.
Direction: the spread widens (rises towards zero or positive) when the swap rate rises relative to the Treasury yield. A more negative spread means swap rates sit further below Treasury yields.
Long the spread: pay fixed on the swap and be long the Treasury, financed in repo. Check: if the spread widens by \(\Delta s\), the pay-fixed swap gains \(NA\Delta S\) and the long Treasury loses \(MD\Delta y\); with the DV01 match \(MD=NA\) the net is \(NA\,\Delta s\) (the derivation card later in this file derives this).
Interviewer follow-up: Why is 'long the spread' not the same as 'receive the swap and short the Treasury'? Answer: the second is short the spread, a common confusion; check the sign with the DV01 signs before quoting.
Legs of a long 10y swap spread: pay fixed swap plus long Treasury financed in repo

front: [Chain: SWAP_SPREAD 2/3] Context: the 10-year USD swap spread has been negative for an extended period (see the earlier card on the structural drivers). Consider the structural drivers that push the swap rate below the Treasury yield: (i) net Treasury issuance, (ii) demand from asset swappers and liability hedgers, (iii) dealer balance-sheet cost under leverage constraints, (iv) the repo-to-SOFR relationship. For each, give the sign of its effect on the spread and the mechanism.
back:
(i) Treasury supply: heavier net issuance raises Treasury yields relative to swaps, pushing the spread more negative. Mechanism: the Treasury curve must clear more duration, and swaps do not carry the same supply.
(ii) Asset-swap and liability hedgers: an investor who buys a fixed-rate asset and swaps it to floating pays fixed in the swap, which pushes the swap rate up and the spread less negative. A pension or insurer with long-dated liabilities usually receives fixed to add duration, which pushes the swap rate down and the spread more negative. The net sign depends on which flow dominates.
(iii) Balance sheet: dealers intermediate swaps and hold Treasuries against them. A leverage ratio charges balance sheet on Treasuries, which makes holding them costly. If dealers must be compensated for holding Treasury inventory, the Treasury yield is pushed up relative to the swap, so the spread falls.
(iv) Repo versus SOFR: a Treasury long is financed in repo and a swap receiver earns SOFR. If repo trades above SOFR, the carry on a long Treasury is worse, so the Treasury is cheaper; a higher repo cost works against the Treasury and pushes the spread more negative.
Interviewer follow-up: Which of these is most sensitive to the eSLR change? Answer: (iii), since the eSLR is a leverage constraint on Treasury intermediation.

front: [Chain: SWAP_SPREAD 3/3] Context: long the 10-year spread on $100 million, DV01-matched, with the spread at minus 15 bp. Approximate the spread DV01 at about $80,000 per bp per $100 million. Carry is the negative of the spread times notional: a spread of minus 15 bp earns about $150,000 a year if the repo and SOFR rates are equal. The spread moves from minus 15 bp to minus 5 bp in a month. What is the P&L, and what is the carry for the month?
back:
Headline: about $0.8 million of spread P&L plus about $12,500 of carry in the month.
Working: spread change \(+10\) bp \(\times\)$80,000 per bp \(= \$0.8\)m. Carry \(= 15\text{ bp}\times\$100\text{m}/12 \approx \$12{,}500\) for the month, assuming repo equals SOFR.
Caveat: repo and SOFR are not equal in practice, and any specialness on the Treasury leg changes the carry. Use the actual repo rate on the specific Treasury.
Where it breaks: the DV01 match only neutralises parallel moves. The Treasury and swap curves at 10 years have different key-rate exposures, so a curve move can produce a spread P&L unrelated to the spread itself.
Interviewer follow-up: How do you hedge the basis risk of a DV01-matched package? Answer: match key-rate DV01 at 2y, 5y, 10y and 30y, not only the 10-year point.
Spread P&L and one-month carry for a DV01-matched $100m long 10y swap spread

front: Derivation: for a DV01-matched long-swap-spread package with a pay-fixed swap of notional \(N\), par swap rate \(S\), fixed-leg annuity \(A\) per unit notional, and a long Treasury of market value \(M\) with modified duration \(D\) and yield \(y\). Show that with \(M D = N A\), a parallel shift in rates leaves P&L zero and a change in the spread \(\Delta s = \Delta S - \Delta y\) gives P&L of approximately \(N A\,\Delta s\).
back:
Step 1, swap leg: a pay-fixed swap of notional \(N\) gains \(N A\,\Delta S\) when the par rate rises by \(\Delta S\), to first order.
Step 2, Treasury leg: a long Treasury of value \(M\) loses \(M D\,\Delta y\) when its yield rises by \(\Delta y\), to first order.
Step 3, total: \(P\&L = N A\,\Delta S - M D\,\Delta y\). Under the DV01 match \(M D = N A\), this is \(N A(\Delta S-\Delta y) = N A\,\Delta s\).
Parallel check: if \(\Delta S=\Delta y\), \(\Delta s=0\), so P&L is zero to first order.
Where it breaks: second order terms (convexity of the Treasury and the swap annuity) and the mismatch of the two curves at the same tenor. The approximation is good for small moves and a single tenor. For \(\$100\)m at a 10-year, \(NA\approx \$80{,}000\) per bp, consistent with the chain card.
Used in the deck for: the swap-spread DV01 in SWAP_SPREAD 3/3.

front: Scenario: the US enhanced supplementary leverage ratio (eSLR) final rule was adopted in November 2025 and takes effect 1 April 2026, with early adoption from 1 January 2026. A trader expects the 10-year swap spread to move to less negative levels because dealers can hold more Treasuries. Give the mechanism for that view, then the counter-argument from the swap side, and say why the net direction is ex-ante ambiguous.
back:
Mechanism for the view: a lower leverage charge on Treasury holdings frees balance sheet for Treasury intermediation and repo. Dealers hold more Treasuries and demand more of them, which lowers Treasury yields relative to swaps. The spread (swap minus Treasury) rises, i.e. less negative.
Counter-argument: derivative exposures also enter the leverage denominator. If the relief also lowers the cost of holding swaps (receiving or paying), dealers will warehouse more swap risk, and the swap rate moves too. Dealers can also hedge their Treasury inventory with swaps, so the two sides are linked.
Ambiguity: the net effect depends on which constraint binds at the margin. Eligible Treasury holdings versus derivative notionals have different balance-sheet weights and netting, so the sign of the spread effect depends on the marginal dealer's portfolio. Ex ante, the sign is not identified from the rule text alone.
Interviewer follow-up: What would you look at to decide? Answer: dealer Treasury inventory and repo volume versus swap notional outstanding, and whether the constraint in the GSIB surcharge is binding on the bank holding company or its subsidiary.

front: Case study: a US dollar investor buys a 10-year JGB at a 1.50% yield and hedges the currency back to USD with a rolling 3-month forward. USD 3-month rate is 4.00%, JPY 3-month rate is 0.75%, and the cross-currency basis for USD-JPY hedges is minus 15 bp (the hedger pays 15 bp extra). Estimate the hedged yield, and explain why hedging adds yield rather than costs it for this investor.
back:
Headline: hedged yield about 4.60%, against 1.50% unhedged.
Working: hedged yield \(\approx y_{JGB} + (r_{USD}-r_{JPY}) + b = 1.50 + (4.00-0.75) + (-0.15) = 4.60\%\), with \(b\) the signed cross-currency basis (negative means the hedger pays).
Why hedging adds yield: the investor holds a low-yielding JPY asset and sells the JPY forward. The forward points embed the rate difference: USD interest is higher, so the forward USD per JPY is above spot, and selling JPY forward locks in the higher rate. The pickup equals the rate differential, which is the carry the investor earns from the hedge.
Caveat: the rate inputs are illustrative. The basis term is what changes with stress, and the pickup disappears if the basis is larger than the rate difference.
Interviewer follow-up: Why do Japanese investors hedge the other way? Answer: a JPY investor holding USD assets earns the USD yield minus the JPY-USD rate differential minus the basis, so the sign of the pickup flips.
Yield bridge: unhedged JGB 1.50% plus rate differential less basis gives 4.60% hedged

front: Derivation: starting from covered interest parity with a cross-currency basis, show that for a USD investor holding a JPY bond at yield \(y\) and hedging with a forward, the hedged USD yield is approximately \(y + (r_{USD}-r_{JPY}) + b\), where \(b\) is the signed basis, added to the hedged USD yield (negative means the hedger pays). State the sign convention and where the approximation fails.
back:
Step 1, forward: with spot \(S\) (USD per JPY) and rates \(r_{USD}\), \(r_{JPY}\) over \(\tau\), covered parity gives \(F = S\,\frac{1+r_{USD}\tau}{1+r_{JPY}\tau}\).
Step 2, basis: with a cross-currency basis \(b\) (negative means the hedger pays), the effective forward is \(F = S\,\frac{1+r_{USD}\tau}{1+(r_{JPY}-b)\tau}\). A negative \(b\) lifts the implied JPY rate in the forward relation, i.e. the hedger pays.
Step 3, hedged return: the JPY coupon \(y\) is converted at the hedge rate, and the forward points add the rate differential less the basis cost. To first order the hedged USD yield is \(y_{hedged}\approx y + (r_{USD}-r_{JPY}) + b\), with \(b<0\) meaning the hedger pays.
Where it breaks: the approximation is first order in \(\tau\) and in the rates. It ignores compounding, the difference between simple and continuous rates, and the time-varying nature of the basis over the bond's life. Over a 3-month roll the error is small, over 10 years the basis changes.
Used in the deck for: the hedged JGB case in the preceding card.

front: Derivation: a 2s5s9s fly with a short Bobl belly (DV01 €51.7 per contract) and long Schatz and Bund wings of €25.9 DV01 each (per the preceding chain). Let \(\Delta y_2,\Delta y_5,\Delta y_9\) be yield moves in bp. Write the P&L as a function of these moves and show that the fly is pure curvature in a level-plus-slope-free sense. What is the residual exposure once the wings' yield betas are not equal to one?
back:
Step 1: a long position of DV01 \(d\) loses \(d\,\Delta y\) in bp terms when yields rise, so \(P\&L = -\sum_i w_i\,\text{DV01}_i\,\Delta y_i\).
Step 2: wings are long (Schatz and Bund, each DV01 €25.9), belly is short (Bobl, DV01 €51.7). \(P\&L = -25.9(\Delta y_2+\Delta y_9)+51.7\,\Delta y_5 = 51.7\left(\Delta y_5-\tfrac{\Delta y_2+\Delta y_9}{2}\right)\).
Step 3, reading: a parallel move gives zero. A pure steepening (2y down 5, 9y up 5, 5y unchanged) gives zero. A belly-only move gives \(51.7\,\Delta y_5\). So the exposure is the 5y against the average of the wings, i.e. curvature.
Where it breaks: the algebra assumes each wing moves one-for-one with its own yield. If the wings' yield betas to the 5y are not 1 (the betas differ by tenor and by regime), the 'average' is a weighted average with unequal weights, and the fly picks up a slope bet. Quantify it with the beta-adjusted weights, not the DV01 weights.
Used in the deck for: the 2s5s9s fly in EURFUT 3/3 and the beta-neutral fly case in the existing deep govies set.

front: Euro-Buxl: the contract's CTD set is small (bonds with 24 to 35 years remaining at delivery, and a 4% notional coupon). Explain why a short futures position is exposed to a delivery squeeze in the Buxl more than in the Bund, what a squeeze looks like in the CTD's price and in the futures-to-cash basis, and what a desk does to manage it.
back:
Why more exposed: a small deliverable set means the cheapest-to-deliver is one or two bonds. If a holder controls a large share of those bonds, the cash price of the CTD can be bid up relative to the futures, so the short cannot buy the bond back at a price consistent with the futures settlement.
What it looks like: the CTD's cash price rises relative to its implied repo-based forward, the implied repo rate on the CTD falls sharply (even negative), and the gross basis narrows or inverts against the shorts. The futures price may move less than the CTD.
How the desk manages it: monitor the implied repo of each deliverable bond against general collateral; size the short against the free float of the CTD rather than the total issue; avoid holding the futures into the last trading day when the CTD is concentrated; and where needed, hedge with the next-cheapest bond or with a cash position in the CTD.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the Bund not have the same problem to the same degree? Answer: its deliverable set is wider in issue count and in tenor, so no single bond is as likely to be a squeeze target.

front: Cloze: the Euro-Schatz future references a remaining term of {{c1::1.75 to 2.25}} years with a {{c2::6%}} notional coupon, and the Euro-Bobl references {{c3::4.5 to 5.5}} years with a {{c4::6%}} notional coupon.
back: Remaining-term and coupon ranges are from the Eurex options contract pages, which list the underlying futures terms (Schatz 1.75 to 2.25 years, Bobl 4.5 to 5.5 years, both 6%). The Schatz minimum price change in the same table is 0.005, worth €5. The Bobl tick is not on this card: the same Eurex table gives 0.005 (€5), which conflicts with the 0.01 (€10) reading, so it is left out until the futures page is checked.

front: Cloze: a DV01 match on the 10-year point of a sovereign or swap package leaves {{c1::key-rate}} exposure at the other tenors unhedged, so a 'DV01-neutral' trade is only {{c2::level-neutral}} to first order.
back: Key-rate DV01 at 2y, 5y, 10y and 30y is the standard check. The phrase 'level-neutral to first order' means parallel moves cancel; slope and curvature are not hedged by one-point matching.
